planting.note: Set divisions into gritty, sharply drained soil tucked among rocks or in crevices in spring, mimicking the cliff and canyon-wall habitat where this species naturally roots.

directions: Mexican cliff fern is a small, tufted fern native to rocky canyon walls and cliff crevices across the southwestern United States and into Mexico, where it anchors itself in thin pockets of soil among sandstone or igneous rock. Its narrow, twice-cut fronds are covered in fine hairs and scales, an adaptation shared with its Woodsia relatives that helps it endure the intense light and periodic drought of exposed rock habitats. In cultivation it is best suited to a crevice garden or rockery with sharp drainage rather than a conventional shade bed, sited where it receives filtered or morning sun. Established plants tolerate considerable summer dryness but should not be allowed to sit in saturated soil over winter.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into rock crevices or scree with sharp drainage in spring; this species roots naturally in shallow pockets on sandstone and igneous cliffs across the Four Corners region.

directions: New Mexican cliff fern occupies rocky cliffs and talus slopes across the Four Corners region and the southern Rockies, often at considerable elevation where it experiences cold winters and intense summer sun. Its compact, scaly rootstock produces tufts of narrow, ladder-like fronds with closely spaced pinnules that distinguish it from several similar southwestern Woodsia species. Like other cliff-dwelling woodsias it is adapted to shallow, mineral soil rather than rich garden loam, and performs best wedged into rock crevices or a well-drained scree bed. Provide protection from prolonged summer wet, which is far more damaging to this species than drought or cold.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a consistently moist, shaded rock crevice or grotto near a seep line, mirroring the sheltered alcoves this fern favors in the wild.

directions: Cochise cliff fern is a sky-island specialist restricted to a handful of shaded canyons in the Arizona-New Mexico borderlands and adjacent Sonora and Chihuahua, where it grows on granite or volcanic ledges and in rock alcoves near springs and seeps. This habitat is notably shadier and more consistently moist than that of most of its Woodsia relatives, which tend toward sunnier, drier cliff faces. Its brittle, straw-colored petioles and sparsely glandular fronds distinguish it from the superficially similar Woodsia plummerae with which it was long confused. Because wild populations depend on a steady seep of moisture, garden specimens appreciate a shaded crevice or grotto setting kept more evenly moist than is typical for the genus.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into cracks and ledges on calcareous rock, such as limestone or dolomite boulders, in a shaded site that stays cool and evenly moist through the growing season.

directions: Laurentian fragile fern is a fertile hybrid derived from bulblet fern and common fragile fern, found growing in rock crevices and on calcareous boulders and cliff ledges scattered across the Great Lakes region and northeastern North America into adjacent Canada. It forms low, arching clumps of twice-divided fronds and occasionally bears the small, irregular bulblets inherited from one parent species along the rachis. Populations are naturally scattered and uncommon, so garden specimens are usually propagated by division rather than collected from the wild. Site it in a shaded limestone or dolomite crevice garden with reliable moisture at the root zone, since it does not tolerate the summer drying that drier-adapted cliff ferns can withstand.

planting.note: Plant divisions into cracks and ledges on calcareous sandstone or limestone in a sheltered, shaded canyon-wall setting, keeping the root zone from drying out completely between waterings.

directions: Utah fragile fern is a rare bladder fern restricted largely to the Colorado Plateau, with a scattering of additional sites in southern New Mexico and adjacent Texas, where it roots in cracks and sheltered ledges on calcareous cliff faces at mid to high elevation. It arose naturally as a hybrid between bulblet fern and Reeves' fragile fern, and its twice-divided fronds carry fine glandular hairs along the main leaf axis that help separate it from the more familiar common fragile fern. In the garden it is best treated like other cliff-crevice ferns, grown in a narrow pocket of gritty, calcareous soil in a shaded canyon-style rock garden rather than open ground. It is slow to establish and should not be collected from wild populations, which are limited and scattered.

planting.note: Plant divisions in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil near streamside rock ledges or on shaded talus, reflecting the boreal seep and streambank habitats this fern favors.

directions: Mountain bladder fern is a boreal species found across subarctic Canada and Alaska, with isolated outlying populations at high elevation in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado and Montana where cool, moist microclimates persist. It spreads by a slender, creeping rhizome rather than forming a tight clump, giving it a looser, more open habit than most other bladder ferns, and its broadly triangular fronds are twice- to thrice-divided. In the wild it favors wet woods, streambanks, and moist rock ledges near or above treeline, so garden success depends on cool summer temperatures and soil that never fully dries out. It is a poor choice for warm-summer gardens and is best reserved for cold-climate or high-elevation plantings with reliably moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade.
